## Why? {#why}

**Research question:** How many participants does the next simulator study need to reliably find a difference that matters for the design?

Studies that are too small miss relevant effects, and if they do become significant, they overestimate the effect. Studies that are too large cost time and participants. A power analysis before the study makes the planning transparent and belongs in every preregistration and ethics application. After the study it is no longer a tool for explaining a result.

## Concept {#concept}

```{=html}
<figure class="rt-figure">
<svg viewBox="0 0 560 190" role="img" aria-labelledby="fig-pwi-title fig-pwi-desc" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">

  <desc id="fig-pwi-desc">Four boxes in a circle: effect size, sample size, alpha and power. In the middle: fix three, compute the fourth.   <rect x="40" y="20" width="130" height="34" rx="4" class="rt-fig-box-accent" />

  <text x="455" y="42" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-label">n</text>
  <rect x="40" y="100" width="130" height="34" rx="4" class="rt-fig-box" />
  <text x="105" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-label">α (usually .05)</text>
  <rect x="390" y="100" width="130" height="34" rx="4" class="rt-fig-box" />
  <text x="455" y="122" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-label">Power (1 − β)</text>
  <text x="280" y="70" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-label">fix three,</text>
  <text x="280" y="88" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-label">compute the fourth</text>
  <text x="105" y="170" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-code">a priori → n</text>
  <text x="280" y="170" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-code">sensitivity → d</text>
  <text x="455" y="170" text-anchor="middle" class="rt-fig-code">simulation → power</text>
</svg>
<figcaption>Effect, sample size, α and power are linked. A priori, you fix effect, α and power and compute n; with a fixed sample you compute the smallest effect it reliably finds. For complex models, power is simulated.</figcaption>

```

- **Smallest effect size of interest (SESOI):** plan from the effect that matters in practice (e.g. 5 SUS points, 40 ms reaction time), not from a pilot effect; those are uncertain and usually too large.
- **pwr** for standard tests: `pwr.t.test()` (independent, paired, `type =`), `pwr.r.test()`, `pwr.anova.test()`, `pwr.f2.test()` (regression). The quantity you leave out is computed.
- **Repeated measures:** for paired tests, d is the difference divided by the SD of the differences (d_z). For several conditions, **Superpower** `ANOVA_design()` + `ANOVA_exact()` computes with means, SD and the correlation `r`; the correlation decides a lot.
- **Mixed models:** no formula. **simr** takes a pilot model, sets the expected effect (`fixef(fit)["x"] <- ...`), extends the design (`extend()`) and simulates (`powerSim()`, `powerCurve()`).
- **Sensitivity instead of "post hoc" power:** after the study, what counts is which effects the design could find (`pwr.t.test(n = ..., power = .8)`) and the CI of the effect. Power computed from the observed effect is just the p-value converted.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## More: equivalence, interactions, your own simulation

- **Planning equivalence:** if you want to show that two prototypes are *equally good*, plan an equivalence test (TOST) with bounds ±SESOI; `TOSTER::power_t_TOST()`. This needs more participants than a difference test.
- **Interactions** need clearly more participants than main effects; in Superpower `design = "2b*3w"` and the row of the interaction in `main_results`.
- **Your own simulation** for any design: generate data with the assumed effect, fit the model, store the p-value, e.g. 1000 times with `replicate()` or `purrr::map()`; the share of p < .05 is the power. simr does exactly this for `lmer()` models.
- **Several tests:** plan for the most important comparison, with a smaller α under Holm correction.
:::

## Example {#example}

How many participants per group does a t-test need for a medium effect (d = 0.5) with 80% power, and which effect does a study with 20 per group reliably find?

```{webr}
pwr.t.test(d = 0.5, power = 0.8)
pwr.t.test(n = 20, power = 0.8)
```

64 participants per group, i.e. 128 in total. With 20 per group, the study has 80% power only from d = 0.91, i.e. only for very large effects. Within participants it looks different:

```{webr}
pwr.t.test(n = 20, power = 0.8, type = "paired")
```

Paired, d_z = 0.66 is enough: the same 20 participants find much smaller differences if each sees all conditions.

**How to report it (methods section):** The sample size was determined a priori with pwr (Champely, 2020). For the smallest difference of interest of 5 SUS points (SD = 12, d = 0.42), a two-sided t-test for independent groups with α = .05 and 90% power requires 123 participants per group.

## Package comparison {#packages}

| Task | Recommendation | Alternative |
|---|---|---|
| t-test, correlation, one-way ANOVA, regression | **pwr** `pwr.t.test()`, `pwr.r.test()`, `pwr.f2.test()` | G*Power (program outside R); `stats::power.t.test()` |
| Repeated measures, mixed ANOVA, contrasts | **Superpower** `ANOVA_design()`, `ANOVA_exact()`, `plot_power()` | your own simulation with afex |
| Mixed models | **simr** `powerSim()`, `extend()`, `powerCurve()` | your own simulation; mixedpower, faux (simulate data) |
| Equivalence | TOSTER `power_t_TOST()` | – |

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Run locally: power curve with simr

In the browser, 50 simulations are a compromise. For real planning, run locally with 1000 runs over several sample sizes (takes a few minutes):

```r
library(simr)
fit <- lmer(rt_ms ~ condition + trial_c + (1 + trial_c | participant), data = sim)
fixef(fit)["trial_c"] <- -15
fit100 <- extend(fit, along = "participant", n = 100)
curve <- powerCurve(fit100, test = fixed("trial_c", "t"), along = "participant",
                    breaks = c(30, 40, 50, 60, 80, 100), nsim = 1000)
plot(curve)
```
:::

## Cheat sheet {#cheatsheet}

```r
# A priori: n from the smallest effect of interest
pwr.t.test(d = 5 / 12, power = 0.9)                    # n per group
pwr.t.test(d = 40 / 90, power = 0.9, type = "paired")  # d_z = diff. / SD of diffs.
# Sensitivity: which effect at a fixed n?
pwr.t.test(n = 40, power = 0.8)

# Repeated measures with correlation
design <- ANOVA_design(design = "3w", n = 20, mu = c(1000, 960, 940),
                       sd = 140, r = 0.85, plot = FALSE)
ANOVA_exact(design, verbose = FALSE)$main_results

# Simulate a mixed model
fixef(fit)["trial_c"] <- -15
fit60 <- extend(fit, along = "participant", n = 60)
powerSim(fit60, test = fixed("trial_c", "z"), nsim = 50)
```
